places.name: Ybor City Historic District
aliases: Ybor City National Historic Landmark District
places.summary: A National Historic Landmark district northeast of downtown Tampa, founded in 1886 as a planned cigar-making town. It keeps cigar factories, immigrant social-club buildings, worker houses and the 7th Avenue commercial strip.
places.quote: At the turn of the 20th century, nowhere in the United States was as famous for its cigars as Tampa’s Ybor City, which was once known as the “Cigar Capital of the World.”

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
National Historic Landmark District
City of Tampa local historic district

heritage.story: In late 1885 Vicente Martínez-Ybor and Ignacio Haya bought land northeast of Tampa for cigar factories and worker housing; by the end of 1886 both factories were running and several hundred worker houses were occupied, and Tampa annexed Ybor City in June 1887. Cuban, Spanish and Italian immigrants built mutual-aid clubs with cooperative medical plans, and José Martí came here to raise money and support for Cuban independence. The hand-rolled cigar industry declined after the 1920s, and a 1965 urban renewal project leveled 70 acres, including 660 frame houses, before preservation efforts turned the district around. The City of Tampa gives its period of significance as 1886 to 1940.
heritage.visiting: Walk the 7th Avenue commercial strip, which the National Park Service says runs 11 blocks from Nick Nuccio Parkway to 26th Street. The Ybor City Visitor Information Center is in the Centro Ybor complex (1600 E 8th Ave, Suite B104; Monday to Saturday 10 AM–4 PM, Sunday noon–4 PM), and the Ybor City Museum State Park is on 9th Avenue.

places.notes: Coordinates are the district point from Wikipedia's NRHP list. Built = the City's period of significance (1886–1940); the NPS says most buildings date from 1886 to World War I. NHL district year 1990 from the City designations book.

places.name: Cuban Club (El Círculo Cubano de Tampa)
places.summary: The four-story clubhouse of El Círculo Cubano, a Cuban mutual-aid society founded in 1902, built in 1917 after fire destroyed the first clubhouse. It is now an event venue with a ballroom, theater, cantina and courtyard.
places.quote: The historic Cuban Club is open to the community as an events center for weddings, business expos, cultural and musical events, and more.

heritage.architect: M. Leo Elliott with Bayar C. Bonfoey
heritage.style: Neoclassical (the NHL nomination calls it Beaux Arts)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: Cuban cigar workers founded El Círculo Cubano in 1902 as a mutual-aid society; its first clubhouse, built in 1907, burned in 1916. The present yellow brick building, finished in 1917 on the same site, held a theater, pharmacy, library, ballroom and cantina, and Hillsborough County says it served as a temporary hospital during the 1918–1920 influenza epidemic. The Cuban Club Foundation was formed in the early 1990s to maintain the building.
heritage.visiting: The club says it does not give public tours; several Ybor ghost and history tours stop here, and its rooms are rented for events. A historical marker stands at East Palm Avenue and Avenida República de Cuba.

places.notes: Dates differ: the club, the county marker and the NHL nomination say 1917; the Ybor Chamber (USF text) says the $60,000 building was completed in 1918. The Chamber dates the predecessor Club Nacional Cubano to Oct 10, 1899.

places.name: El Centro Español de Tampa
places.summary: The 1912 clubhouse of El Centro Español, the mutual-aid society Spanish immigrants incorporated in 1891, and a National Historic Landmark. The restored building is the centerpiece of Centro Ybor, a shopping and entertainment complex that opened in 2000.
places.quote: El Centro Espanol de Tampa is the best surviving Spanish ethnic and cultural club building in the Gulf Coast States that were the main focus of immigration from Spain in the last decades of the 19th century

heritage.style: Mediterranean Revival (French Renaissance Revival with Moorish and Spanish influences)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
National Historic Landmark
Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: El Centro Español, incorporated in December 1891, was the first ethnic club in Ybor City; by 1908 it had 2,687 members, and the NHL nomination calls its 1906 Sanatorio probably the most modern hospital in Florida at the time. The club put up this dark red brick building in 1912 with a cantina, theater and ballroom, and sold it in 1983. After years of vacancy the building was restored, and Centro Ybor opened around it in 2000. The society still exists as a heritage organization.
heritage.visiting: The building is part of Centro Ybor on 7th Avenue (shops, restaurants, entertainment); the Ybor City Visitor Information Center is in the same complex at 1600 E 8th Ave, Suite B104.

places.notes: Architect from the NPGallery record for 88001823 (Kennard, Francis J.). NHL year 1988 = NRHP/NHL listing date 6/3/1988 on NPGallery.

places.name: Centro Asturiano de Tampa
places.summary: The clubhouse of a mutual-aid society founded in 1902 by immigrants from Asturias, Spain, completed in 1913–1914 with a theater, ballroom and cantina. It hosts events and offers a free one-hour history tour on Tuesdays at 10 a.m.
places.quote: The Centro Asturiano de Tampa was a social club for immigrants and the descendants of immigrants from Asturias, Spain.

heritage.architect: M. Leo Elliott and B. C. Bonfoey
heritage.style: Beaux Arts characteristics (NHL nomination); the club calls it Renaissance Mediterranean

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: In 1902 a group of 546 immigrants from Asturias founded the club as a branch of the Centro Asturiano de La Habana; membership brought hospital, cemetery and health benefits. After fire destroyed its earlier clubhouse at Palm and Nebraska, members built the present three-story yellow brick and stone building for $110,000. Its theater, which the NHL nomination counts at 1,062 seats, drew zarzuela companies and performers such as Ernesto Lecuona. The NHL nomination notes that the building has never been vacant.
heritage.visiting: Free history tours every Tuesday at 10 a.m. (about one hour; sign up online). The club says the tour covers the building's history, not its event spaces; venue tours are by phone.

places.notes: The NHL nomination's club table dates the society to 1902 (the NPS lesson plan says 1904); the club says 1902.

places.name: Italian Club of Tampa (L'Unione Italiana)
places.summary: The 1918 clubhouse of L'Unione Italiana, the mutual-aid society Italian immigrants founded in Ybor City in 1894. It is a membership club and event venue with a theater, ballroom and cantina.
places.quote: Founded on April 4, 1894, the Club was created by Italian immigrants who came together to support one another, preserve their heritage, and build a better life in Tampa.

heritage.architect: M. Leo Elliott and B. C. Bonfoey
heritage.style: Neoclassical (NHL nomination); the club cites Italian, Spanish and Greek influences

designations.name: Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: L'Unione Italiana was founded on April 4, 1894, by 116 Italians and eight Spaniards, with Bartolomeo Filogamo as its first president. Its first clubhouse, across 7th Avenue, opened in 1912 and burned in May 1914. Construction of the present building began in April 1917 and it was completed in 1918, with a theater and balcony, ballroom, cantina, library and space for members' medical services.
heritage.visiting: The club is a membership organization and event venue; its site invites visitors to call (813) 248-3316 about a tour.

places.notes: Costs differ: the club says about $120,000; the Ybor Chamber (USF text) says $80,000 with furnishings; left out. The club page says the building is on the National Register; it is a contributing building of the Ybor City district (no individual NRHP listing in Wikipedia's list).

places.name: V. M. Ybor Cigar Factory (Ybor Factory Building)
places.summary: The red brick cigar factory Vicente Martínez-Ybor completed in 1886, the first factory of the planned town of Ybor City. José Martí spoke from its 14th Street steps in 1893; the building is now privately owned offices.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: Ybor's factory at 14th Street and 9th Avenue was completed in 1886; a second factory (the Stemmery) and a warehouse followed in 1902, filling most of the block between 8th and 9th Avenues and 13th and 14th Streets. In 1893 José Martí spoke from the factory's cast-iron steps, urging cigar workers to join the fight for Cuban independence; the original portico was taken to Havana and the present one is a reproduction. After Ybor died in 1896 the plant passed to the Havana America Company (1899), the American Cigar Company (1901) and Hav-A-Tampa (1954), and in the 1970s it became the Ybor Square shopping mall.
heritage.visiting: Private property: view the exterior and the reproduction portico on 14th Street (Avenida República de Cuba). Wikipedia reports that the building became offices in 2002 and that the Church of Scientology bought it in 2010.

places.notes: Address left null: sources give 1911 N 13th St (Wikipedia) and 1910–1916 Avenida Republica de Cuba / 14th Street (NHL nomination, HABS). Point is the OSM building 'Ybor Square'.

places.name: El Pasaje (Cherokee Club)
places.summary: A two-story red brick building across 9th Avenue from the Ybor factory, built for the Cherokee Club, a men's social club whose guests included Grover Cleveland. It has held a hotel, restaurants and offices; view it from the street.

heritage.style: Renaissance (an Italian palazzo, per the NHL nomination)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: The NHL nomination says Vicente Martínez-Ybor and Eduardo Manrara erected the building in 1895 to house the Cherokee Club, which accepted both Latin and American members and offered rooms to members and guests including Grover Cleveland, Gen. Leonard Wood and the artist Frederick Remington. When completed it was only the second brick building in Ybor City. Its arcade of 38 arched brick columns lines the ground floor, and a restoration was completed in 1988.
heritage.visiting: Private building; the arcaded facades face 9th Avenue and 14th Street. Wikipedia says it now houses the headquarters of a technology company.

places.notes: Wikipedia says built 1886 and names TheIncLab as the tenant; TheIncLab's contact page lists 1320 E 9th Ave (next address), not 1318.

places.name: Parque Amigos de José Martí
places.summary: A small walled park on the site of the home of Ruperto and Paulina Pedroso, Black Cubans who sheltered José Martí in 1893. It was developed in 1960, has a statue of Martí, and is technically Cuban property, according to the NHL nomination.

heritage.story: The park occupies the site of the house of Ruperto and Paulina Pedroso, two Black Cubans who sheltered Martí when Spanish assassins were sent to Ybor City in search of him in 1893. The house burned in the late 1950s and the park was developed in 1960; it has a larger-than-life statue of Martí and a plaque with a medallion portrait of Paulina Pedroso. USF Libraries records that Los Libres Pensadores, forerunner of La Unión Martí-Maceo, held its first official meeting at the Pedroso home on October 26, 1900.
heritage.visiting: An open-air park at 8th Avenue and 13th Street, a block from the Ybor factory; the Martí statue and Pedroso plaque are inside the walls.

places.notes: Opening hours not found on an official page.

places.name: La Unión Martí-Maceo
places.summary: The clubhouse of Tampa's Afro-Cuban mutual-aid society, named for Cuban patriots José Martí and Antonio Maceo. Its first clubhouse on 6th Avenue was demolished in 1965 during urban renewal; the society then moved into this 1950 building on 7th Avenue.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark
Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: Segregation split the Club Nacional Cubano, which had served Black and white Cubans, into the Círculo Cubano and Los Libres Pensadores Martí-Maceo, whose first official meeting took place on October 26, 1900, at the home of Ruperto and Paulina Pedroso; it later merged with La Unión, an Afro-Cuban society in West Tampa. Its clubhouse at 1907–1909 E. 6th Avenue was demolished in 1965 during urban renewal. The society moved into this converted commercial building, which has a tile panel celebrating its namesakes; the NHL nomination classes it as contributing to the district because of its exceptional importance.
heritage.visiting: View the exterior and its tile panel on 7th Avenue.

places.notes: Dates differ: the City book says the members relocated here in 1966; the NHL nomination says the club acquired the building in 1960. The NHL club table dates La Unión Martí-Maceo to 1904 (first building 1909). No official website found; whether the building is open to visitors is not stated.

places.name: Columbia Restaurant (Ybor City)
places.hours_text: Sunday–Thursday 11 AM–9 PM; Friday–Saturday 11 AM–10 PM.
places.summary: A Spanish restaurant that grew from a corner saloon opened in 1903 and became the Columbia Restaurant in 1905; it now fills a city block of 7th Avenue. The restaurant says it is Florida's oldest restaurant.
places.quote: The 1903 corner saloon transformed into the Columbia Restaurant in 1905, using the same iconic bar.

heritage.built: 1903 (saloon); expanded to its present size by the 1930s; tiled arcade 1963

designations.name: Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: Casimiro Hernandez Sr., a Spanish-Cuban immigrant, helped open the Columbia Saloon on December 17, 1903, and it became the Columbia Restaurant in 1905; the original bar is still in the Cafe dining room. The NHL nomination says the restaurant had taken on its present dimensions by the 1930s and that its latticed arcade with a red tile roof dates to 1963; inlaid tiles around the windows and doors show flowers, animals and scenes from Spanish history. The restaurant is still owned and run by the founder's family.
heritage.visiting: Open daily for lunch and dinner; the restaurant says it seats up to 1,700 in 15 dining rooms across 52,000 square feet.

places.notes: Heritage record for the eat-tampa id; restaurant details (menu, reservations) belong to eat-tampa. Point is the OSM restaurant feature. The NHL nomination spells the founder 'Casimirio'; the restaurant spells it Casimiro.

places.name: Tampa Theatre
places.summary: A 1926 atmospheric movie palace designed by John Eberson, rescued from demolition in the 1970s and now a nonprofit film and concert house. Its auditorium is built to look like a Mediterranean courtyard under a night sky.
places.quote: When Tampa Theatre opened in 1926 it was the city's first commercial building to offer air conditioning.

heritage.style: Atmospheric movie palace (the City of Tampa lists it as Mediterranean Revival)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Designed by John Eberson, the theatre opened on October 15, 1926, inside a ten-story office building on Franklin Street; its auditorium imitates the garden of a Spanish villa under a ceiling of stars, and its Wurlitzer organ is still played. Attendance declined in the 1960s and 1970s and in 1973 the building faced demolition; the City of Tampa rescued it by taking over its leases, the Arts Council of Hillsborough County ran its programming from 1976 to 2010, and it reopened in early 1978. A 2017 renovation reseated the auditorium, reducing capacity from 1,446 to 1,238 seats.
heritage.visiting: See a film or concert, or join one of the building tours the theatre offers (Visit Tampa Bay lists tours among its 600-plus yearly events). The National Register plaque is on the front of the box office; the Franklin Street box office is open 10 AM–6 PM on weekdays.

places.notes: Heritage for the shared venues-bay id. The City designations book says 'Constructed: 1925'; the county and Wikipedia give the 1926 opening. tampatheatre.org returned 202/empty to both curl and WebFetch, so it is only the url. Visit Tampa Bay's listing text says both 600+ and 1,000+ events a year.

places.name: Tampa City Hall (Old City Hall)
places.summary: Tampa's 1915 Beaux Arts city hall, whose clock tower made it a focal point of the early skyline. It still houses city government, including City Council offices on the third floor.

heritage.architect: B. C. Bonfoey and M. Leo Elliott (builder McGucken & Hyer)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Ground was broken in 1914, and the City of Tampa says the finished building was the tallest south of Jacksonville, with a tower that made it a focal point of the skyline. Its Seth Thomas clock is named for Hortense Oppenheimer, who led the effort to raise money for a public clock like those she had seen in northern cities. The building was documented by the Historic American Buildings Survey in 1981 and renovated in 2017.
heritage.visiting: A working government building; see the clock tower from Kennedy Boulevard and Florida Avenue.

places.notes: The OSM feature named 'Tampa City Hall' is the 306 E Jackson St building; the point here is the census match for 315 E Kennedy Blvd.

places.name: S. H. Kress & Co. Building
places.summary: A 1929 Renaissance Revival department store with terra cotta facades on both Franklin Street and Florida Avenue, on the 'Kress block' it shares with the former Woolworth and Newberry stores. View it from the street; the block's owner has announced plans to preserve and redevelop it.

heritage.architect: G. F. McKay (builder G. A. Miller)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: S. H. Kress opened its first Tampa store in 1904; this building, with nearly identical facades on Franklin Street and Florida Avenue faced in terra cotta that imitates granite, was one of downtown's most popular stores for decades. The block it shares with the former F. W. Woolworth and J. J. Newberry stores is known as the Kress block; students' 1960 lunch-counter sit-ins at the Woolworth store are marked on the corner of Polk and Franklin. Wikipedia reports that the Wilson Company bought the block in 2017 with plans to preserve and redevelop it.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only; walk both the Franklin Street and Florida Avenue facades.

places.notes: Addresses: NRHP 811 N Franklin St; the City book lists the landmark at 810 N Florida Ave (the other facade). Architect spelled G.F. McKay (City book), G. E. McKay (NPGallery) and G.E. Mackey (Wikipedia). Current use of the Kress building not found; the county says the neighboring Woolworth store is vacant.

places.name: Woolworth Sit-In Site (former F. W. Woolworth store)
places.address: N Franklin St at E Polk St
places.summary: The former Woolworth store on Franklin Street where about 40 Black high school students began daily lunch-counter sit-ins on February 29, 1960. A two-sided historical marker at Polk and Franklin names the participants.
places.quote: By September 1960, Tampa's lunch counters were integrated without the violence that marked desegregation efforts in many other parts of the country.

heritage.story: On February 29, 1960, about 40 students from George S. Middleton and Howard W. Blake high schools, led by NAACP Youth Council president Clarence Fort and NAACP state president the Rev. A. Leon Lowry, sat in at the Woolworth lunch counter. After about a week of demonstrations Mayor Julian B. Lane agreed to appoint a biracial committee, and by September 1960 Tampa's lunch counters were integrated. Hillsborough County says the store closed in the early 1990s and the building is vacant; the marker was erected in 2018.
heritage.visiting: Read the marker on the corner of East Polk Street and North Franklin Street (on the right when traveling west on Polk); it is a Soulwalk stop.

places.notes: The store's address differs: the City's Soulwalk page says 901 N. Franklin St.; the county marker inscription says 801 North Franklin Street. The point is the census match for 801 N Franklin St, next to the Kress Building (811).

places.name: Sacred Heart Catholic Church
places.hours_text: Mass Monday–Friday 7 AM and 12:10 PM; Saturday vigil 5:30 PM; Sunday 7:30, 9 and 10:30 AM, noon and 5:30 PM.
places.summary: A granite and white marble Romanesque church dedicated in 1905 on the site of the 1859 frame church of St. Louis Parish. Its 70 stained glass windows were made by Franz Mayer of Munich; it is an active Franciscan parish.
places.quote: The Romanesque architecture remains. The exterior is a combination of granite and white marble.

heritage.story: A frame church named St. Louis was built on this site in 1859, and the parish was constituted in 1860. Jesuits took over the parish in 1888 after yellow fever killed three pastors; they broke ground for the present church on February 16, 1898, and dedicated it on January 15, 1905, renaming the parish Sacred Heart. Jesuit High School began in the church's sacristy in 1899. Franciscan friars took over the parish in 2005.
heritage.visiting: An active parish; visitors are welcome at Mass (weekday Masses at 7 AM and 12:10 PM).

places.notes: Architect (Nicholas J. Clayton of Galveston) is from Wikipedia; the parish history page does not name him.

places.name: St. Andrew's Episcopal Church
places.summary: Tampa's first Episcopal congregation (1871) worships in this 1907 Mediterranean Revival church at Marion and Madison streets, designed by Miller & Kennard. It reuses stained glass windows from the parish's earlier wooden church.

heritage.architect: Michael J. Miller and Francis J. Kennard

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa multiple property designation: North Franklin Street / Downtown

heritage.story: The congregation was established on July 24, 1871, and first worshiped in a hospital building at Fort Brooke; it bought this block in 1877 and built a wood frame church in 1883. Construction of the present building began in 1904 and was finished in 1907, reusing the stained glass windows, communion rail and lectern of the wooden church.
heritage.visiting: An active parish; the church is on the corner of Marion and Madison streets.

places.notes: The parish domain listed on Wikipedia (saintandrewstampa.org) now serves unrelated spam; no official site found. The City book lists the church at 501 N. Marion St. (constructed 1907) in the North Franklin Street / Downtown multiple property designation.

places.name: Tampa Union Station
places.hours_text: Station open 9:45 AM–6 PM daily (Amtrak agents on duty).
places.summary: An Italian Renaissance Revival railroad station opened in 1912 that still serves Amtrak's daily Floridian between Chicago and Miami. Restored by volunteers and reopened in 1998, it is also an event venue; the Friends of Tampa Union Station say a renovation is under way.
places.quote: Tampa Union Station is a fully operational train station that has been a gateway to the city for over a century.

heritage.architect: J. F. Leitner (builder W. C. Hobbs)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Designed by J. F. Leitner of Wilmington, North Carolina, the station opened on May 15, 1912, to combine the passenger operations of the Atlantic Coast Line, the Seaboard Air Line and the Tampa Northern Railroad; the City notes it was built by a group of businessmen led by Peter O. Knight rather than a railroad company. Its waiting room was segregated when it opened. Ridership fell after the 1950s and the station closed in 1984; a volunteer-led nonprofit raised over $4 million, restoration was completed in May 1998, and CSX donated the station to the City of Tampa that year.
heritage.visiting: The waiting room is open when Amtrak agents are on duty (9:45 AM–6 PM daily). Limited free parking at the station; the City's Twiggs Street Garage is nearby.

places.status_note: Friends of Tampa Union Station's site says a renovation is under way ('Stay tuned for updates once the station's current renovation is complete'); train service continues daily.
places.notes: NRHP date: NPGallery 6/5/1974; the Friends' history page says February 2, 1974. The segregated waiting room is from Wikipedia.

places.name: Jackson Rooming House
places.summary: A two-story boarding house a block from Union Station that lodged Black travelers, railroad workers and touring musicians during segregation. The City says it is the only such boarding house left standing in Tampa; a foundation is working to stabilize and restore it.
places.quote: Properties like the Jackson Boarding House played a crucial role during the segregation era, and though it was not the only boarding house (or hotel) for Blacks visiting Tampa, it is the only one that remains standing.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Moses and Sarah Jackson built the house as their residence (the foundation says 1901; the City dates Moses Jackson's purchase to 1899) and expanded it into a boarding house near Tampa Union Station, which opened in 1912. Because African Americans were barred from white hotels until the early 1960s, it housed Black railroad workers, servicemen and entertainers; the foundation lists guests including Count Basie, Cab Calloway, Ella Fitzgerald, James Brown and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. The family ran it as a boarding house into the 1990s.
heritage.visiting: Not open to the public; see the exterior and the Soulwalk marker in front of the house.

places.notes: End of boarding use: the City's Soulwalk page says the 1990s; Wikipedia says 1989. Wikipedia (citing news reports) describes stalled restoration and a 2023 City Council land-swap vote with a neighboring parking owner; status as of Sep 2026 not confirmed on the foundation site, which asks for help to 'Stabilize and Restore' the house.

places.name: North Franklin Street Historic District
places.summary: A National Register district of early-20th-century commercial buildings at the north end of downtown's Franklin Street, the last surviving part of Tampa's early downtown business district.

heritage.style: Commercial styles of the early 20th century

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa multiple property designation: North Franklin Street / Downtown

heritage.story: The City of Tampa says these buildings are the last surviving elements of the early downtown business district, which began before 1900 and peaked in the 1930s, serving residents who lived between the Hillsborough River and Nebraska Avenue. The National Register district, listed on March 28, 2002, is bounded by Florida Avenue and East Fortune, Tampa, Franklin and East Harrison streets. The National Register nomination notes that the land boom slowed in 1926, when financial backing for the Davis Islands real estate venture collapsed.
heritage.visiting: Walk North Franklin Street between Harrison and Fortune streets; the buildings are private.

places.notes: The NRHP form counts 8 contributing buildings and a period of significance of c. 1903–c. 1921. City local designation years for the grouping span 2003–2017.

places.name: Masonic Temple No. 25 (Hillsborough Lodge No. 25)
places.summary: A 1928 Mediterranean Revival Masonic lodge by architect M. Leo Elliott, a lodge member, with terra cotta details showing the gavel, plumb, square, level and trowel. It is still the lodge's meeting place, with shops on the ground floor.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Hillsborough Lodge No. 25 chose Elliott, one of its members, to design a building for ceremonial, administrative and commercial uses; its terra cotta ornament depicts the builders' tools that are Masonic symbols. The cornerstone of the lodge's fourth building was laid on June 18, 1928, and the first meeting in the new temple was held on February 19, 1929.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only, at the corner of Kennedy Boulevard and Morgan Street.

places.notes: Wikipedia says 'Erected in 1927' but also gives the June 18, 1928 cornerstone; the City book says constructed 1928.

places.name: Kennedy Boulevard Bridge (Lafayette Street Bridge)
places.summary: The 1913 bascule bridge carrying Kennedy Boulevard over the Hillsborough River between downtown and the University of Tampa, the third bridge at the city's first river crossing. The City of Tampa calls it the oldest bascule span in Florida.

heritage.architect: Edwards Construction Company; Oswego Bridge Company

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa multiple property designation: Historic Bridges on the Hillsborough River

heritage.story: The first bridge over the Hillsborough River, the Lafayette Street Bridge of 1888, linked the City of Tampa with Hyde Park and the site of Henry Plant's Tampa Bay Hotel. The 1913 span is the third bridge built at this crossing and one of six Hillsborough River bridges from 1913 to 1939 in a City of Tampa historic designation.
heritage.visiting: Cross it on foot between downtown and the University of Tampa; the Hillsborough River bridges are listed together in a City of Tampa historic designation.

places.notes: NRHP listing 2018-02-20 per Wikipedia's list (NPGallery shows no date). Builders from the NPGallery 'Architects' field.

places.name: Historical Monument Trail (Tampa Riverwalk)
places.summary: Bronze and marble busts and monuments along the Tampa Riverwalk honoring 30 people and events from Tampa and Hillsborough County history, from the Mound Builders to Ybor City's founders, chosen from 2012 to 2017.
places.quote: the Historical Monument Trail of beautiful bronze and marble busts and monuments tells the story of many noteworthy people and the significant events that have shaped the history of Tampa and Hillsborough County.

heritage.story: The Friends of the Riverwalk and the Tampa Bay History Center set up a committee of local experts that chose 30 honorees from 2012 through 2017. They include Florida's First People (the Mound Builders), Gavino Gutierrez, Ignacio Haya, Paulina Pedroso, Clara C. Frye, Blanche Armwood, Hugh Campbell Macfarlane and Peter Oliphant Knight.
heritage.visiting: Free and outdoors along the Riverwalk; the Friends of the Riverwalk site has a biography of each honoree.

places.notes: No coordinates: the page does not say where along the Riverwalk the monuments stand. Visit Tampa Bay says there are over 30 monuments and that they are built to the height of the individuals (not stated by the Friends' page).

places.name: Cotanchobee Fort Brooke Park
places.summary: A 4.5-acre waterfront park on the Garrison Channel, named for Fort Brooke, the Army post of 1824 around which Tampa grew. It has a memorial to the Seminole Indian Wars, a cenotaph by Native American artist Bob Haozous, a playground and splash pad, and the Riverwalk's end point.

heritage.story: In January 1824 Col. George Mercer Brooke arrived in Tampa Bay with four companies of infantry under orders to establish a military post; the fort served as a garrison for the Seminole Wars, and the village of Tampa grew up beside it. According to Wikipedia, most of the fort's structures stood where the Tampa Convention Center is now. The park's stainless steel and bronze cenotaph by Bob Haozous honors the dead whose remains lie elsewhere.
heritage.visiting: Open 7 AM–10 PM; next to the Tampa Bay History Center, with an overlook, a canoe launch and boat slips (72-hour limit).

places.notes: GPS coordinates published on the City page. Fort location relative to the park from Wikipedia (Fort Brooke); fritzhand/history-of-tampa puts the fort site about 613 m west of the park. Arrival date: the City archive says January 18, 1824; Wikipedia says the cantonment was established January 10, 1824.

places.name: Perry Harvey Sr. Park
places.summary: A city park on the edge of the old Central Avenue business district, the heart of the Black neighborhood known as The Scrub. Timeline pavers, historic-photo LIFETILES and a Leaders' Row tell the area's history, and the skate park replaces the 1970s Bro Bowl.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Perry Harvey Sr. Park Skateboard Bowl)

heritage.story: The Scrub, Tampa's oldest and largest African American neighborhood, grew up after the Civil War around the Central Avenue Business District. Its single-family homes were demolished in 1959 for the Central Park Village housing project, and I-4 and 1960s urban renewal disrupted Central Avenue; the Encore development later replaced Central Park Village. The park's original skateboard bowl, opened in 1979 and listed on the National Register in 2013 as the first skatepark on a national register, was demolished in a park renovation and replaced by a design based on it.
heritage.visiting: Open sunrise to 10 PM; follow the timeline pavers and LIFETILES history walk, see the gateway sculptures of musicians and dancers, and skate Bro Bowl 2.0.

places.notes: GPS coordinates published on the City page. Whether the NRHP listing survives the bowl's demolition is not stated; the verifier should check.

places.name: Oaklawn Cemetery
places.summary: Tampa's first public burying ground, established in 1850 for 'white and slave, rich and poor', with the adjoining Catholic St. Louis Cemetery (1874). Tampa's first mayor and 12 other mayors, a Florida governor and Ybor City founder Vicente Martínez-Ybor are buried here.
places.quote: Tampa's first public cemetery (1850) represents every level of society, from enslaved people to governors.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The Alachua County Commission established Oaklawn as a public burying ground on April 1, 1850, when Tampa had about 500 people; a portion was set aside for enslaved people. In 1874 the Leonardi family donated adjoining land for the Catholic St. Louis Cemetery. Many early markers were carved cypress and were lost to fire, rot and storms, and the original plat was misplaced after the Civil War; the Sexton's House dates to 1910 and the receiving vault to 1894. The City lists about 1,700 known burials.
heritage.visiting: Open 8 AM–6 PM daily; the City publishes a self-guided walking tour of 20 stops. It asks visitors not to touch markers, make rubbings or step inside plot enclosures.

places.notes: Ybor's burial in the St. Louis section is from Wikipedia. NRHP 2017 (the City page; Wikipedia gives Sept 19, 2017 in text and 2017-09-25 in its list).

places.name: St. Paul A.M.E. Church
aliases: St. Paul African Methodist Episcopal Church
places.summary: A 1917 Gothic Revival church built for one of Tampa's oldest Black congregations, where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Mary McLeod Bethune and Jackie Robinson addressed the congregation. The building now serves the residents of the Metro 510 apartments.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Established in the late 19th century, St. Paul A.M.E. played a central role in Tampa's African American community and by the late 1960s was one of the city's oldest and strongest religious organizations. The City of Tampa records that Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Mary McLeod Bethune and Jackie Robinson addressed the congregation. The Gothic Revival building now holds a community center, leasing office, fitness room and library for the Metro 510 residential community.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only.

places.notes: Address: City book 502 E. Harrison St.; the OSM feature is on N Marion St at the same corner. Where the congregation worships today is not stated in the book.

places.name: St. Peter Claver Catholic School
places.summary: A 1929 brick school building, one of the few survivors of The Scrub neighborhood, home to what the City of Tampa calls the oldest African American school still operating in Hillsborough County.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The main building is one of the few historic structures left in The Scrub; an annex was added on its east side in 1952 for a growing enrollment, and both have been little altered. The City of Tampa says St. Peter Claver is the oldest African American school still in operation in Hillsborough County.
heritage.visiting: A working school; view from the street.

places.notes: The school's own site was reachable but not read for history.

places.name: Robert W. Saunders, Sr. Public Library
places.summary: A public library in the old Scrub neighborhood, named for the NAACP Florida field director Robert W. Saunders Sr., with exhibits on the Civil Rights movement and an interactive History of Central Avenue hallway.
places.quote: This library contains many museum quality exhibits, including displays on the Civil Rights movement and the NAACP located in the lobby.

heritage.story: The branch began in 1933 as the Ybor City Branch Library in a storefront donated by the Italian Club; a building at 1505 N. Nebraska Avenue was dedicated in January 1969. On November 5, 2003, the county renamed it for Robert W. Saunders Sr., civil rights activist and former NAACP field director. Wikipedia reports that the 1969 building was replaced by a new two-story library that opened in August 2015, keeping a bronze bust of Saunders and the stone mural Symbols of Mankind.
heritage.visiting: Free; open Monday to Saturday. The Civil Rights and NAACP displays are in the lobby and the History of Central Avenue hallway has touch panels with audio and video.

places.notes: HCPLC's history paragraph stops at the 1969 building; the 2015 replacement and its architect are from Wikipedia. is_free left null (library visits are free by nature, but the page does not say so).

places.name: Tampa Heights Historic District
places.summary: One of Tampa's earliest residential neighborhoods, just north of downtown, with brick streets, granite curbstones and houses in Colonial Revival, Queen Anne, Tudor Revival and Mediterranean Revival styles. It is a National Register and City of Tampa historic district.

heritage.style: Colonial Revival, Queen Anne, Tudor Revival, Mediterranean Revival

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic district

heritage.story: Tampa Heights grew with the prosperity of the late 19th century, when former wilderness and farmland became streets of large houses; urban professionals chose it for its architecture and its closeness to downtown. The City's local district covers about 200 acres, with 282 contributing buildings and a period of significance of 1890 to 1945, and keeps original brick streets, granite curbstones and stamped concrete sidewalks.
heritage.visiting: A residential neighborhood; the National Register district is roughly bounded by Adalee Street, I-275, 7th Avenue and North Tampa Avenue (per Wikipedia's NRHP list). The houses are private.

places.notes: Coordinates: the district point from Wikipedia's NRHP list; boundaries from the same list.

places.name: Old Tampa Free Public Library
places.summary: A Carnegie-funded Classical Revival library of 1915 designed by Fred J. James, Tampa's main library until 1968. It now holds library administrative offices; see it from the street.

heritage.architect: Fred J. James (builder Aulic, Bastes & Hudnell)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The City of Tampa says this was the second of two Tampa libraries built with Carnegie Foundation grants and that it served the public for more than 50 years. Wikipedia reports that construction was completed in 1915 but the library did not open until April 27, 1917, after a dispute over its operating budget, and that it was Tampa's main library until the new downtown library opened in 1968.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only; Wikipedia says the Tampa-Hillsborough County Public Library administration has occupied it since 2016.

places.notes: Wikipedia also says the building houses the City's Community Affairs Department in one passage and library administration in another; current tenant not confirmed on an official page.

places.name: Woodlawn Cemetery
places.summary: Tampa's second municipal cemetery, established in 1888 and now the largest City-owned cemetery. Its 40 acres take in six burial grounds, including Jewish, Spanish and carnival workers' (Showmen's Rest) sections.
places.quote: Tampa's second municipal cemetery (1888) spans 40 acres and includes six separate burial grounds, including Jewish, Spanish, and carnival worker sections.

heritage.story: Woodlawn was established in 1888 as Tampa's second municipal cemetery. Privately owned cemeteries adjoin it, including Schaarai Zedek, Rodeph Sholom, Beth Israel and Showmen's Rest, and the City took over the Pyramid Crypts section in late 2023. Named plots include the Pioneer Garden, the Old People's Home memorial, the Children's Home memorial and the Hampton family crypts.
heritage.visiting: Open 8 AM–6 PM daily; the entrance is at West Indiana Avenue and North Ola Avenue. The City publishes a cemetery map.

places.notes: The City's cemetery page spells it 'Schaari Zedek'. Location 'West Indiana Ave & North Ola Ave' is from the Soulwalk cemeteries page.

places.name: Buffalo Soldiers in Tampa Heights historical marker
places.address: E Columbus Dr at N Central Ave
places.summary: A 1998 historical marker at Columbus Drive and Central Avenue recalling the Black regiments, the Buffalo Soldiers, who camped on the edge of Tampa Heights in 1898 before sailing to Cuba in the Spanish-American War.

heritage.story: Hillsborough County hosted over 30,000 troops in 1898. Ten regiments, including two Black units, camped on the fringes of Tampa Heights: the Twenty-fourth Infantry just north of the marker and the Twenty-fifth to the southeast. The marker says the soldiers met hostility in Tampa, that a serious clash between Black and white troops took place on the eve of embarkation, and that the Buffalo Soldiers earned five Medals of Honor at San Juan and El Caney.
heritage.visiting: The marker is at East Columbus Drive and North Central Avenue, on the left when traveling east on Columbus Drive.

places.notes: Erected by the Hillsborough County Historical Advisory Council and the Tampa Historical Society.

places.name: St. James House of Prayer Episcopal Church
places.summary: A 1922 Gothic Revival church in Tampa Heights built with chert, a native stone, as a structural material. It is home to a parish formed in 1997 by the merger of the House of Prayer and St. James, a congregation organized in 1892 for Tampa's Black Episcopalians.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The House of Prayer congregation was organized in 1908 and grew under William Conckling Richardson, which led to this sanctuary; through the 1920s and 1940s it was the third largest Episcopal church in Tampa. The City of Tampa says it is one of two identified buildings in Florida built with chert as a structural material. Wikipedia reports that in 1997 the congregation merged with St. James Episcopal Church, founded in 1892 to serve Tampa's Black population, whose site was taken for the new Blake High School.
heritage.visiting: An active parish on Central Avenue; view the stone exterior from the street.

places.notes: Founding year of the House of Prayer: the City says organized in 1908; Wikipedia says founded 1907. Wikipedia says the stone was collected from the Hillsborough River (text truncated in the fetched copy; not used).

places.name: Old Hillsborough County High School (D. W. Waters Career Center)
places.summary: The 1911 Classical Revival building of Hillsborough County's earliest high school, designed by William Potter. It still houses a public school, the D. W. Waters Career Center.

heritage.architect: William Potter (1923 addition by M. Leo Elliott)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Hillsborough County High School, the county's earliest high school, opened here in 1911; a 1923 addition by M. Leo Elliott partly filled the building's open center. It later housed Thomas Jefferson Junior High (1928–1938) and Jefferson High School (until 1967), and in 2002 it was renamed the D. W. Waters Center for an educator who served as a principal for 41 years. It now specializes in career education.
heritage.visiting: A working school; view from the street.

places.notes: NRHP year: NPGallery 5/15/2007; the City book says 2008.

places.name: Ulele (Tampa Water Works building)
places.summary: A restaurant and brewery that opened in 2014 in Tampa's 1902 Water Works pumping station on the Hillsborough River, next to the restored Ulele Spring and Water Works Park. It is run by the Columbia Restaurant Group.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The City of Tampa built this steam-powered pumping station to bring fresh water to its residents; it raised the city's spring water capacity to four million gallons a day. The building was rehabilitated to the Secretary of the Interior's Standards for adaptive reuse in 2014, and the adjacent Ulele Spring was restored and reconnected to the Hillsborough River. The restaurant says it opened in August 2014.
heritage.visiting: Open for lunch and dinner; the spring is beside the restaurant and Water Works Park next door.

places.notes: Heritage for the restaurant record (eat-tampa may use this id; if it uses another, merge). Restaurant hours are left to eat-tampa: the FAQ gives Sun–Thu 11–10, Fri–Sat 11–11 but may be old.

places.name: Seminole Heights Historic District
places.summary: An early streetcar suburb north of downtown with oak-shaded streets lined with Craftsman bungalows built between 1912 and 1939. It is a National Register and City of Tampa historic district.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic district

heritage.story: Seminole Heights was developed outside the city limits along the trolley line from Tampa north to Sulphur Springs. The City's local district covers about 215 acres, with 374 contributing buildings, mostly bungalows built between 1912 and 1939, many of them elaborately detailed. Wikipedia notes that the district also includes Hillsborough High School and Seminole Heights United Methodist Church.
heritage.visiting: A residential neighborhood, roughly between Hanna and Osborne avenues and Florida and Cherokee avenues (per Wikipedia); the houses are private.

places.notes: Wikipedia counts 325 contributing buildings in the national district; the City counts 374 in the local district.

places.name: Sulphur Springs Water Tower
places.summary: A 214-foot Gothic Revival water tower of 1927 on the banks of the Hillsborough River, the landmark of the old Sulphur Springs resort. The City of Tampa says it is one of only two architecturally designed water towers in Florida.
places.quote: The Sulphur Springs Water Tower is one of the few remnants of a successful tourist and recreation center that flourished around a naturally bubbling spring and included a direct street car line from Tampa.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Josiah Richardson built the 214-foot tower over a spring on the Hillsborough River, with a 150,000-gallon tank; it was the area's main water source until the early 1970s. By the 1920s Sulphur Springs was a popular destination reached by streetcar from Tampa, with medicinal waters, an alligator farm, a pool, a toboggan slide and a dance hall. Richardson also built the octagonal 1925 gazebo over the spring itself (701 E. Bird Street), a separate City landmark.
heritage.visiting: See it from North Florida Avenue near the Hillsborough River.

places.notes: The City book gives 'National Register Listing: 1989', but the tower does not appear in Wikipedia's NRHP list for Tampa; the verifier should find the NRHP reference or drop that designation. The see-tampa slice has sulphur-springs-museum.

places.name: Babe Zaharias Golf Course
places.summary: A public golf course laid out in 1925, bought in 1949 by Babe Didrikson Zaharias and her husband George, and reopened by the City of Tampa in 1974 under her name. It is managed by the Tampa Sports Authority.
places.quote: Known in the Tampa Bay area as "The Babe," Babe Zaharias Golf Course was named after Mildred Ella "Babe" Didrikson Zaharias

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Designed in 1925 by J. Franklin Meehan for Burks L. Hamner's Forest Hills development, the course opened as the Northside Country Club and was soon renamed Forest Hills. George Zaharias bought it in 1949, and he and Babe, an Olympic champion and co-founder of the LPGA, ran it until 1955, when they moved to Texas after her cancer diagnosis. The City of Tampa took it over and reopened it in 1974 as the Babe Zaharias Golf Course; a county historical marker was added in 2023.
heritage.visiting: Public golf; book tee times through the Tampa Sports Authority. The historical marker is on the course grounds.

places.notes: The developer is spelled 'Burks L. Hammer' on the marker and 'B.L. Hamner' in the City book.

places.name: Rogers Park Golf Course
aliases: Original Rogers Park Golf Course Site
places.summary: An 18-hole public course on the Hillsborough River, built from 1948 to 1952 as the only golf course open to Tampa's Black residents during segregation. Its original site is on the National Register; the Tampa Sports Authority runs it.
places.quote: Built in 1952, Rogers Park Golf Course has evolved as one of Tampa's best kept secrets.

heritage.architect: Willie Black (first head golf professional, with volunteers)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Original Rogers Park Golf Course Site)

heritage.story: The City of Tampa acquired land by the river after World War II for a park for Black residents, named for businessman G. D. Rogers in 1951. Caddies led by Willie Black, the first head golf professional, cleared the course; a nine-hole course opened around 1952 and was later expanded to 18 holes. Wikipedia lists Charlie Sifford, Ted Rhodes and Charles Owens among the Black golfers who played it.
heritage.visiting: Public golf with a driving range and a short course; book tee times on the course site.

places.notes: History is mainly from Wikipedia (citing Tampa Tribune articles); the course site says only 'Built in 1952', 160 acres, 18 holes. NRHP listing 2014-11-12 per Wikipedia's list; NPGallery shows no date. Address: NRHP 7801 N 30th St; Wikipedia gives 7911 Willie Black Drive (no census match).

places.name: West Tampa Historic District
places.summary: The core of West Tampa, a cigar-making city incorporated in 1895 and annexed by Tampa in 1925, with cigar factories, ethnic social clubs, a Carnegie library and hundreds of cigar workers' houses. Brick streets, granite curbs and hexagonal sidewalk pavers survive.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa multiple property designation: West Tampa

heritage.story: Hugh C. Macfarlane set out to turn 120 acres of swampland west of the Hillsborough River into a cigar town; his investment company financed the Fortune Street Bridge and built factories and worker housing, and by 1893 West Tampa had 25 cigar factories. It incorporated as a city in 1895, with a population largely of Spanish, Italian and Cuban immigrants, and stayed independent until Tampa annexed it in 1925. Hillsborough County notes that it then had the second largest Hispanic population in Florida.
heritage.visiting: Start at Main Street and Howard Avenue, the old commercial core; the Carnegie library, El Centro Español de West Tampa and several cigar factories are on Howard Avenue.

places.notes: Period of significance 1894–1945 is the City's for its West Tampa multiple property grouping (local designations 2006 and 2022). The NRHP district is roughly bounded by Cypress and Ivy streets and Fremont and Habana avenues (Wikipedia list).

places.name: El Centro Español de West Tampa
aliases: El Centro Espanol of West Tampa
places.summary: The 1912 West Tampa clubhouse of the Spanish mutual-aid society, with patterned dark red and yellow brick and terra cotta tracery in a Moorish Revival style. It now houses the offices of the Hillsborough Education Foundation.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark
West Tampa Historic District (National Register)

heritage.story: Built as an ethnic club for the immigrants of the City of West Tampa, El Centro Español offered low-cost family medical care, education, recreation, entertainment and citizenship programs. Wikipedia reports that the building stood empty for years, was restored by the City of Tampa, served as a temporary home for the Tampa Museum of Art, and was leased in 2010 to the Hillsborough Education Foundation.
heritage.visiting: Office building; view the facade on Howard Avenue.

places.notes: Current tenant: the Hillsborough Education Foundation lists 2306 N. Howard Ave. as its address.

places.name: West Tampa Branch Library (Carnegie library)
places.summary: A 1913 Classical Revival Carnegie library built by the City of West Tampa on land donated by cigar manufacturer Angel Cuesta, still in use as a public library. The City of Tampa calls it Tampa's first free public library.

heritage.architect: John W. Biggar (builder G. A. Miller)

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark
West Tampa Historic District (National Register)

heritage.story: The City of West Tampa built the library with a grant from the Carnegie Foundation, one of ten Florida public libraries Andrew Carnegie funded, on land given by Angel Cuesta. It linked the town, the cigar industry and its immigrant community, and it still offers materials in Spanish. A 5,000-square-foot addition was completed in 2003 and the original building was refurbished in 2004.
heritage.visiting: Free; open Monday to Saturday. Artworks by Ferdie Pacheco hang in the foyer and a stained glass installation lines the west wall.

places.notes: The City book lists the landmark at 1718 N. Howard Ave. (National Register 1983, as part of the West Tampa district); the library gives 2312 W. Union St. as its address.

places.name: Fort Homer W. Hesterly Armory (Shanna & Bryan Glazer JCC)
places.summary: An Art Deco National Guard armory built on the site of a Rough Riders camp from the Spanish-American War, later a concert and speaking hall that hosted John F. Kennedy, Martin Luther King Jr. and Elvis Presley. Since 2016 it has been a Jewish community center.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The Florida National Guard armory stored arms and provided drill space and was renamed for Col. Homer Wynne Hesterly soon after completion. It also served as a venue for sports, social and speaking events, hosting President John F. Kennedy, Martin Luther King Jr. and Elvis Presley, according to the City of Tampa. After the Guard left, the building reopened on December 8, 2016, as a Jewish community center, renamed the Shanna and Bryan Glazer JCC in 2023.
heritage.visiting: A membership community center (fitness, aquatics, arts, events); contact the JCC about visiting.

places.notes: Built: the City book says 1941; Wikipedia says built in the 1930s and dedicated the day after Pearl Harbor; NPGallery lists 1938 as a significant year.

places.name: Sicilian Club
places.summary: The 1929 Mediterranean Revival clubhouse of West Tampa's Sicilian mutual-aid society, with blond and red brick detailing and a theater at the rear. The club merged with Ybor City's Italian Club in 1934.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark
West Tampa Historic District (National Register)

heritage.story: The Sicilian Club was one of Tampa's original ethnic clubs, offering members the same cradle-to-grave benefits as the Ybor City clubs, and its rear theater staged entertainment for West Tampa. The Italian Club's history says the Sicilian Club of West Tampa merged with L'Unione Italiana in 1934, creating a combined membership of more than 3,000.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only, on Howard Avenue.

places.notes: Current use of the building not found. NRHP 1983 in the City book = the West Tampa district listing.

places.name: Berriman-Morgan Cigar Factory
places.summary: A 1904 brick cigar factory on Howard Avenue, built and run by the Berriman Brothers until 1911 and by the Morgan Cigar Company until the mid-1960s. Rehabilitated in 2008, it is now a college campus.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark
West Tampa Historic District (National Register)

heritage.story: Berriman Brothers built and operated the factory until 1911, and the Morgan Cigar Company occupied it through the mid-1960s. The City of Tampa calls it an excellent example of the design and function of West Tampa's cigar factories. After an extensive rehabilitation in 2008 it became a college campus.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only.

places.notes: The City book does not name the college.

places.name: Bustillo Brothers & Diaz Cigar Factory
places.summary: A three-and-a-half-story yellow brick cigar factory of 1902 with red brick Renaissance Revival trim, where Bustillo Brothers & Diaz made the Henry the Fourth, Alexander Humboldt and Flor del Mundo brands.

heritage.architect: M. J. Miller and Francis J. Kennard

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark
West Tampa Historic District (National Register)

heritage.story: In 1902 Bustillo Brothers & Diaz needed a larger, more modern building than their wood frame factory, and local architects Miller & Kennard drew the plans. A high parapet with a corbelled brick cornice hides the gabled roof, and a classical portico shelters the entrance.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only.

places.name: Balbin Brothers Cigar Factory
places.summary: A 1904 brick cigar factory built for the Samuel I. Davis Company and occupied by the Balbin Brothers from 1911 through the 1930s; West Tampa still calls it the Balbin Brothers building.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark
West Tampa Historic District (National Register)

heritage.story: Like most cigar factories of its time, the building pairs a practical plan with a facade in a popular style. Cigar makers often moved from building to building while making the same label; this one was built for the Samuel I. Davis Company, and the Balbin Brothers used it from 1911 through the 1930s.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only.

places.name: MacFarlane Park
places.summary: A West Tampa city park whose hilltop octagonal pavilion (1924) and red and blond brick gateway (mid-1930s) were the setting for many of the community's social events. The historic structures are a City of Tampa landmark.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: A new octagonal pavilion replacing a wooden predecessor was unveiled at the park's dedication in 1924, and it served as the venue for many West Tampa social activities. The red and blond brick gateway at the main entrance was built in the mid-1930s.
heritage.visiting: A public park; the gateway marks the main entrance.

places.notes: No City park page found for hours or amenities.

places.name: Martí-Colón Cemetery
places.summary: West Tampa's cemetery, begun in 1896 as the West Tampa Cemetery, where headstones with decorative tile reflect the neighborhood's immigrant heritage. The City of Tampa now owns both its parts, Martí and Colón.
places.quote: Originally West Tampa Cemetery (1896), this cemetery honors José Martí and features headstones with decorative tile reflecting West Tampa's immigrant heritage.

heritage.story: Usually called Martí-Colón, it is two cemeteries: the northern Martí Cemetery, privately owned until the City bought it in the 1930s, and Colón Cemetery, parcels that lessee A. P. Boza Sr. bought and turned into burial plots. The City purchased the Colón parcels in May 2023 and now owns both.
heritage.visiting: Open 8 AM–6 PM daily.

places.name: Cespedes Hall historical marker
places.address: N Albany Ave near W Main St
places.summary: A 2024 marker for Cespedes Hall, the wooden hall (1895–1898) that served as West Tampa's first city hall and a base for Cubans supporting the war for independence from Spain. The building is gone; the marker stands near Albany Avenue and Main Street.

heritage.story: La Sociedad Patriótica Céspedes de West Tampa paid $20,000 to build the hall, which also held a school, West Tampa's government offices, an opera hall and businesses. West Tampa's first mayor, Fernando Figueredo Socarrás, named it for his mentor Carlos Manuel de Céspedes, hero of Cuba's Ten Years' War, and it became a rallying point for workers who gave money and time to the 1895 independence war. The City of West Tampa demolished the wooden building in late 1898, likely for fear of fire.
heritage.visiting: The marker is on North Albany Avenue near Main Street.

places.notes: Erected in 2024 by the Hillsborough County Historical Advisory Council. The point is the Albany/Main intersection.

places.name: Fortune Taylor Bridge (Laurel Street Bridge)
places.address: W Laurel St at N Doyle Carlton Dr
places.summary: A 1927 drawbridge over the Hillsborough River, renamed in 2017 for Fortune Taylor, a formerly enslaved woman whose homestead land on the east bank became Fortune Street. A 2018 marker at the west end tells her story.

designations.name: City of Tampa multiple property designation: Historic Bridges on the Hillsborough River

heritage.story: Fortune and Benjamin Taylor married as free people in Tampa on May 5, 1866, and Benjamin claimed a 33-acre homestead on the east side of the river, where they grew oranges, guavas and peaches; after his death Fortune was granted the homestead in 1875. The street through the property was named for her, and the first Fortune Street Bridge, financed by Hugh C. Macfarlane, was built in 1892 to help West Tampa's cigar industry. A tugboat knocked that bridge off its foundation in 1901; the present drawbridge was begun in 1924, completed in 1927, and renamed the Fortune Taylor Bridge in 2017. Fortune Taylor died in 1906 and is buried in Oaklawn Cemetery.
heritage.visiting: The marker is at West Laurel Street and Doyle Carlton Drive, on the right when traveling west on Laurel Street.

places.notes: The City book dates the Fortune Taylor (Laurel Street) Bridge to 1927 and calls its overhead counterweight single-leaf bascule unusual. Area: the marker is on the west bank next to Julian B. Lane Riverfront Park.

places.name: Hyde Park Historic District
places.summary: About 600 acres of late 19th- and early 20th-century revival-style houses and bungalows on tree-lined streets between the Hillsborough River, the bay and Howard Avenue. It is a National Register and City of Tampa historic district.

heritage.style: Late Victorian, revival styles and bungalows

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic district

heritage.story: O. H. Platt bought 20 acres of the Robert Jackson homestead in 1886 and subdivided it into residential lots; after the Tampa Bay Hotel opened in 1891, Hyde Park drew prominent residents. The first bridge over the Hillsborough River, the Lafayette Street Bridge of 1888, linked it to the City of Tampa. The local district, expanded in 2023, counts 918 contributing buildings, including schools, churches and commercial buildings as well as houses.
heritage.visiting: Walk the streets west of the University of Tampa toward Hyde Park Village and Bayshore Boulevard; the houses are private.

places.notes: Summary boundaries from Wikipedia's NRHP list (Hillsborough River and Bay, Howard Ave, Kennedy Blvd); 600 acres from the City book.

places.name: Peter O. Knight Cottage
places.summary: The 1889 Folk Victorian 'honeymoon cottage' of Tampa lawyer and civic leader Peter O. Knight, now the headquarters of the Tampa Historical Society.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark
National Register of Historic Places (listed 1985 per the City of Tampa; Hyde Park Historic District year)

heritage.story: Peter O. Knight practiced law in Tampa from 1889 and was one of the city's early professional and community leaders. He and his wife, Lillie Frierson, lived in this cottage from 1889 to 1900 before moving to a larger house; its gingerbread trim is a modest nod to the Victorian style.
heritage.visiting: Headquarters of the Tampa Historical Society; contact the society about visiting.

places.notes: The City book gives 'National Register Listing: 1985' (the Hyde Park district year). The Tampa Historical Society's web domains did not resolve, so no hours were found.

places.name: Plant Park
places.summary: The riverfront garden Henry B. Plant laid out beside his Tampa Bay Hotel, now part of the University of Tampa campus next to Plant Hall and the Henry B. Plant Museum. The university says it is Tampa's oldest public park.
places.quote: Plant Park is Tampa’s oldest public park and was designated a local historic landmark in 2001.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: In 1886 Plant bought land on the Hillsborough River from Jess Hayden, whose house stood in an orange grove; when hotel construction began in 1888 much of the grove was kept, and Plant set aside 60 acres for a garden of streams, ponds and some 150 varieties of rare and exotic plants. The university says the original Victorian strolling garden is still intact, and the Friends of Plant Park restored parts of it from 1993 to 2018.
heritage.visiting: Open to walk on the University of Tampa campus; a waterfront walkway links it to the Tampa Riverwalk. The Henry B. Plant Museum is in Plant Hall beside it.

places.notes: Area: UT and Plant Hall are in downtown-tampa per SPEC §4.1. The park is a local landmark per UT; the City's 2024 book lists the Tampa Bay Hotel / Plant Hall (1989) rather than the park separately. Build years are the hotel construction years.

places.name: Old School House
places.summary: A small school building from the 1850s, one of the oldest buildings in Tampa, later used by the Tampa Bay Hotel and cared for by the Daughters of the American Revolution since 1931. It stands on the University of Tampa campus.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The City of Tampa calls it the first freestanding, publicly accessible school house built in Hillsborough County; it was built as a school for girls, then served as an outbuilding of the Tampa Bay Hotel and later as a civic meeting space. In 1931 the DeSoto Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution asked Mayor McKay to save it, and the City gave it to the chapter on condition that it be restored and used as a meeting place and museum.
heritage.visiting: Wikipedia says it is open by appointment and during twice-yearly open houses.

places.notes: Wikipedia says it has been moved twice from its original site in what is now Plant Park.

places.name: Stovall House
places.summary: A 1909 Neoclassical mansion on Bayshore Boulevard, home for 30 years of Tampa Tribune founder Wallace F. Stovall and one of the few grand early houses left on the bayfront. View it from the street.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Logan T. and Florence M. Trousdale built the house in 1909 and sold it in 1915 to Wallace F. Stovall, founder and longtime publisher of The Tampa Tribune, who lived here for 30 years and built several of the best-known buildings of the 1920s downtown skyline. Most of the grand houses that once lined Bayshore have been replaced by newer homes and high-rise condominiums.
heritage.visiting: View it from the Bayshore Boulevard sidewalk; the City book does not say whether it is open to visitors.

places.notes: Current use not stated in the sources read.

places.name: Palma Ceia Spring (Fred Ball Park)
places.summary: A small bayside park around a walled natural spring that drew swimmers from about 1903, when Thomas and Ruby Palmer opened Palmera Spring. The spring still flows; a 2025 marker tells how it gave the Palma Ceia neighborhood its name.

heritage.story: Thomas and Ruby Palmer welcomed visitors to their spring-fed pools, a three-mile streetcar ride along Bayshore from downtown, and are credited with naming the area Palma Ceia. A large pool was built in 1928; the county bought the land in the mid-1940s and named it Fred Ball Park, and the City of Tampa acquired it in 1955. Polluted groundwater and backyard pools led to the pool's closing, and volunteers from the Tampa Garden Club's Rose Circle later restored one of the springs with a fountain, walkway and benches.
heritage.visiting: A small public park on Bayshore Boulevard; the spring is inside a concrete wall and the marker is in the park.

places.name: Palace of Florence Apartments
places.summary: A 1925 Mediterranean Revival apartment building with a four-story battlemented tower, modeled on Florence's Palazzo Vecchio as part of D. P. Davis's plan for an Italian-style island suburb. It is private apartments.

heritage.architect: M. Leo Elliott, from a concept by artist Athos Menaboni (builder Island Construction Co.)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Mediterranean Revival Style Buildings of Davis Islands MPS)
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: Developer D. P. Davis turned Big and Little Grassy Islands into Davis Islands in the 1920s and built in the Mediterranean Revival style throughout. Italian-born artist Athos Menaboni conceived this building, using the Palazzo Vecchio and Palazzo del Podestà as inspiration; its north and south sections are divided by a recessed tile-paved courtyard. The National Register nomination for North Franklin Street notes that financial backing for the Davis Islands venture collapsed in 1926.
heritage.visiting: Private apartments; view it from Davis Boulevard.

places.notes: Architect: the City book names M. Leo Elliott; NPGallery lists Menaboni, Athos et al. Wikipedia counts 28 units and a 2002–2003 restoration.

places.name: Palmerin Hotel
places.summary: A 1925 Mediterranean Revival hotel by architect Martin L. Hampton, one of the most visible survivors of D. P. Davis's original Davis Islands. It is now an elder care facility.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Mediterranean Revival Style Buildings of Davis Islands MPS)
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The City of Tampa counts the Palmerin among 20 remaining Mediterranean Revival buildings on Davis Islands listed on the National Register as examples of Florida's 1920s boom, and calls it one of the most important visible survivors of the subdivision founded by D. P. Davis.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only; it houses an elder care facility.

places.name: Roy Jenkins Pool
places.hours_text: Tuesday–Thursday 7 AM–7 PM; Friday 7 AM–noon and 2:30–7 PM; Saturday 7 AM–4 PM; Sunday 10 AM–4 PM; closed Monday.
places.summary: A 1929 Mediterranean Revival public pool on Davis Islands, modeled on Venetian pools and renamed in 1965 for swim-safety leader Roy Jenkins. The City of Tampa runs it year-round.

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The Davis Islands Swimming Pool was the last of the islands' large public projects and, per the City, was modeled after the Venetian Pools in Italy. In 1965 it was renamed for Roy Jenkins, a longtime community leader in youth and aquatic safety.
heritage.visiting: Open year-round for lap swim, open swim and lessons (schedule on the City's pool page); it has an ADA lift and a kiddie pool.

places.name: Cuscaden Park and Pool
places.status_note: The City's pool page says Cuscaden Pool is closed for the season (as of September 2026).
places.summary: A Works Progress Administration park and Art Deco swimming pool of the late 1930s, built on the old Cuscaden orange grove north of Ybor City. The oval pool, designed by engineer Wesley Bintz, is still a City of Tampa pool.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The park and pool were built on land from the Cuscaden Orange Grove as a WPA project. Engineer Wesley Bintz used his patented oval pool plan here, as at pools across the country with different facades. The pool gave Ybor City residents relief from the summer heat, and the park's field was home to the popular Inter-Social Baseball League for many years; the NHL nomination notes a surviving Depression-era baseball grandstand.
heritage.visiting: The pool opens seasonally (zero-entry and ADA lift); check the City's pool schedule.

places.notes: The City book gives NRHP 1990 (likely as part of the Ybor City district boundary increase; no individual listing in Wikipedia's list).

places.name: Our Lady of Perpetual Help Church
places.summary: Ybor City's Catholic church, a buff brick Romanesque Revival building of 1937 that replaced a wooden church of 1891, which had served Catholics of all nationalities with sermons in English, Spanish and Italian.

designations.name: Contributing building, Ybor City Historic District (National Historic Landmark)

heritage.story: The first church on the site, a wooden building of 1891, preached in English, Spanish and Italian. The present church has a three-story tower, a tri-arched entrance, the stone seal of the Redemptorist congregation and stained glass windows; the rectory (1940) and the former St. Joseph's Academy stand on the same block.
heritage.visiting: An active parish; the church is on 11th Avenue at 17th Street.

places.notes: No parish website read; Mass times not included. The NHL text says the church is at the corner of 11th Avenue and '7th Street' (a typo for 17th).

places.name: 1937 Antifascist Women's March marker and mural
places.summary: A 2023 marker and a 'No pasarán' mural on 7th Avenue recalling May 6, 1937, when thousands of Ybor City Latinas marched to City Hall against fascism in Spain.

heritage.story: On May 6, 1937, some 5,000 Latinas from Ybor City gathered on 7th Avenue and marched to downtown Tampa to present Mayor R. E. L. Chancey with a petition supporting Spain's Republic. During the Spanish Civil War the community sent food, clothing, 20,000 cigars, four ambulances, an X-ray machine and medicine to Republican forces, and 24 Ybor men joined the Abraham Lincoln Brigade. Michelle Sawyer's mural shows Dolores Ibárruri, Luisa Moreno and Margot Falcón Blanco.
heritage.visiting: The marker stands in front of the Ybor City Development Corporation building; the mural is on its west wall.

places.notes: The county page gives the crowd as 'thousands' in its text and 5,000 in the marker inscription.

places.name: Memorial Park Cemetery
places.address: 2425 E Dr Martin Luther King Jr Blvd
places.summary: A 20-acre cemetery founded in 1919 for African American World War I veterans, which became the main burial ground for Tampa's Black community under segregation. The City of Tampa bought it in 2023.
places.quote: Established in 1919 for African American WWI veterans, this 20-acre cemetery became the primary burial ground for Tampa's Black community during the segregation era.

heritage.story: Segregation barred Black funerals from Tampa's growing number of private white cemeteries, and the city-owned cemeteries and the Black-owned Zion Cemetery were running out of room. After Memorial Park opened, Tampa's other Black cemeteries were acquired by white interests and their graves removed or built over; Memorial Park remained the only surviving Black cemetery until Zion and others were rediscovered in 2019 and 2020. The City began maintaining it in 2019 after its owner died and bought it in 2023; it holds nearly 20,000 known burials.
heritage.visiting: Open 8 AM–6 PM daily; the City takes requests to help locate a burial.

places.notes: The Soulwalk cemeteries page gives the location as MLK Jr. Blvd & North 22nd Street.

places.name: Tom Henderson Memorial Chapel (First United Methodist Church)
places.summary: A 1948 Late Gothic Revival chapel, the oldest building of the downtown First Methodist Church, which the City of Tampa calls Tampa's oldest church (established 1846).

designations.name: City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: After a rudimentary chapel at Fort Brooke washed away in the Great Gale of 1848, Tampa's Methodists built the city's first official church building, the 'Little White Church', at Morgan and Lafayette streets. The congregation moved to this site in 1891. The chapel, designed by Tampa architect Leslie N. Iredell, keeps its original exterior and interior design and is a rare Late Gothic Revival building downtown.
heritage.visiting: Part of an active church campus; view from Tyler Street.

places.notes: The OSM feature 'First United Methodist Church' sits on the same block; the book calls it 'First Methodist Church'.

places.name: First Federal Savings & Loan Association of Tampa building
places.summary: A 1963 International Style bank building by Harry A. MacEwen, with a glass and marble base and a tower that seems to float over it. It was listed on the National Register in 2018 for its mid-century modern design.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa local historic landmark

heritage.story: The steel frame allowed a curtain wall of plate glass and Mondragone marble, framed in emerald pearl granite, around the three-story base, with ribbons of brick and glass wrapping the tower; the inset fourth story, clad in dark aluminum, makes the tower appear to hover. MacEwen opened his Tampa office in 1959 and designed more than 250 buildings for financial institutions.
heritage.visiting: Exterior only.

places.notes: NRHP listing 2018-10-17 per Wikipedia's list; the City book says NRHP 2018.

places.name: Upper North Franklin Street Commercial District
places.summary: A small National Register district of early-20th-century storefronts on North Franklin Street between Oak Avenue and Kay Street, at the edge of Tampa Heights, including buildings by architects Fred James and Francis J. Kennard.

heritage.architect: Fred J. James; Francis J. Kennard (among others)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
City of Tampa multiple property designation: North Franklin Street / Downtown

heritage.story: The district is bounded by East Oak Avenue, North Florida Avenue, Kay Street and North Tampa Street.
